moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues that contradictory operations involving actual infinities make an infinite past impossible, intending to establish that the temporal universe must have begun.
moves.lockedProposition: An actually infinite past is impossible, so the series of past events and the universe must have begun.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: that the existence of an actually infinite number of things leads to self-contradictions for example what is infinity minus infinity well mathematically you get self-contradictory answers this shows that Infinity is just an idea in your mind not something that exists in reality David Hilbert perhaps the greatest mathematician of this Century States the infinite is nowhere to be found in reality it neither exists in nature nor provides a legitimate basis for rational thought the role that remains for the infinite to play is solely that of an idea but that entails that since past events are not just ideas but are real the number of past events must be finite therefore the series of past events can't go back forever rather the universe must have begun to
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig articulates an inference from contradictory instantiated infinity, using infinity-minus-infinity indeterminacy and Hilbert’s authority, through finitely many past events to the universe’s beginning. Principal limitation: Mathematical nonuniqueness neither demonstrates metaphysical inconsistency in concrete infinities nor licenses transferring abstract cardinal behavior to temporal reality; moreover, a beginning leaves divine causation unestablished. Live burden: Craig must justify that abstraction-to-instantiation bridge across temporal theories, while Flew must explain specifically why the purported contradictions cannot constrain an actually infinite history.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Flew argues that explanation must terminate somewhere and may reasonably stop at the Big Bang, resisting Craig’s inference from cosmic beginning to divine cause.
moves.lockedProposition: Explanations necessarily terminate in brute facts, so the Big Bang may be the justified stopping point rather than requiring a divine cause.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: point every explanation of um why anything is the case is given an answer in terms of something else some general or more General law which at that stage is taken as a brute fact the fact that explains other things now this is surely of the nature of the case you cannot have an end to all explanation that is anything other uh than brute facts of course uh some people find some sorts of brute facts satisfactory to them and they think that's a good place to stop uh but um it doesn't mean that you're able to say it's absolutely wrong to stop at that point so it seems to me uh that you can't rule out uh the possibility that our knowledge of the universe all our knowledge must stop with the big bang that this itself is
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew contests Craig’s transcendent-cause inference by reasoning that explanatory chains terminate in brute facts and the Big Bang could be the epistemic terminus, blocking progression from cosmic beginning to divinity. Principal limitation: Necessary termination does not establish the universe as an appropriate brute fact, and shifting between knowledge’s endpoint and metaphysical explanation’s endpoint obscures the unsupported stopping criterion. Live burden: Flew must justify stopping cosmically without special pleading, while Craig must demonstrate that a timeless cause improves explanation instead of relocating its demand.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Craig combines a universal causal premise with the universe’s beginning, inferring a powerful timeless, changeless, immaterial cause and carrying his central theistic burden.
moves.lockedProposition: Because whatever begins to exist has a cause and the universe began, the universe has a powerful timeless, changeless, immaterial cause.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: thus far as follows premise one Whatever begins to exist has a cause two the universe began to exist three therefore the universe has a cause now from the very nature of the case as the cause of space and time this cause must be an uncaused Timeless changeless and immaterial being of
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig makes the inference auditable by numbering the premises that whatever begins to exist has a cause and that the universe began, then connecting the inferred cause’s relation to spacetime with timelessness, changelessness, immateriality, and power. Principal limitation: He gives insufficient warrant for extending causation to spacetime’s boundary, while a cause’s existence cannot establish every creator-like attribute without bridging arguments. Live burden: Craig must defend that domain extension and derive each attribute without equivocation, while Flew must explain how a beginning universe could lack a cause.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Flew contends that explaining a temporal beginning through an eternal person conflicts with the temporal reasoning Craig used to demand an explanation initially.
moves.lockedProposition: Explaining the universe's temporal beginning by an eternally existing being is inconsistent with the temporal argument used to demand an explanation.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: um uh if um uh uh time uh had to have a beginning um how do we explain that Beginning by saying oh well um uh uh the beginning was started off the whole universe was created by a being uh well um uh that being yes existed eternally well if this argument about uh uh time uh couldn't have uh uh couldn't have if time couldn't have had a beginning uh then uh how is it that as it well a funny sort of time of which of course none of us have ever had an experience um which well uh uh yes of course this it never had a beginning and it will never have an end you know simply won't do uh the argument that gets us to the creation um is inconsistent with the desired explanation of it so I think again it
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew attacks Craig’s personal-cause bridge by arguing that explaining a temporal effect through an eternal being conflicts with the reasoning used to demand explanation of the universe’s beginning. Principal limitation: The objection conflates beginningless duration with timeless existence and offers no warrant that an agent cannot produce a temporal effect without determining conditions, leaving the contradiction unproved. Live burden: Flew must specify why timeless personhood is incoherent, while Craig must explain agency and the effect’s onset without introducing temporal change into the cause.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Craig contrasts impersonal sufficient conditions with free agency, inferring that only personal choice lets a timeless cause produce a universe beginning in time.
moves.lockedProposition: Only a personal agent freely choosing without prior determining conditions can produce a temporal universe from a timeless cause.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: Timeless cause give rise to a temporal effect like the universe if the cause were an impersonal set of necessary and sufficient conditions then the cause could never exist without the effect if the cause were timelessly present then the effect would be timelessly present as well the only way for the cause to be timeless and for the effect to begin to exist in time is for the cause to be a personal agent who freely chooses to
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig’s contrast infers personhood from causal structure: timelessly sufficient impersonal conditions would coexist with their effect, whereas libertarian choice could originate a temporal universe without determining conditions. Principal limitation: This comparison neither demonstrates coherent timeless deliberation nor excludes indeterministic, relational, or nonpersonal causal structures capable of producing a first temporal effect. Live burden: Craig must explain how a timeless agent exercises intention and prove the alternatives exhaustive; Flew must answer why an eternally sufficient impersonal cause would not entail an eternal effect.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Flew limits the experiential causal principle to events within the universe, arguing that extending it to the whole universe’s origin is arbitrary.
moves.lockedProposition: The causal principle is experiential rather than logical and applies within the universe, so extending it to the whole universe is arbitrary.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: has a cause yes absolutely this is not a truth of logic however uh this like the uh principle that every event has a cause is um an experienced truth within the universe and it is wholly arbitrary
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew separates logical necessity from experiential regularity, observing that known causes concern intracosmic events and thereby challenging Craig’s extrapolation to the universe’s beginning. Principal limitation: This distinction defeats deductive certainty but does not show that beginning to exist becomes explanatorily irrelevant at the cosmic boundary; moreover, “arbitrary” understates Craig’s independent metaphysical intuition. Live burden: Flew must identify which constitutive feature of intracosmic causation disappears in cosmic origination, while Craig must justify a non-temporal causal relation without depending on spacetime-bound experience.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Craig invokes metaphysical intuition and uniform experience that beginnings have causes, intending to bar Flew from treating the Big Bang as an unexplained terminus.
moves.lockedProposition: A beginning universe cannot be the brute stopping point, because the causal principle is supported by metaphysical intuition and uniform experience.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: that whatever begins to exist has a cause Dr flu has to refute that first premise if he thinks that the universe is going to be the brute fact and the start stopping point that first premise I think has two lines of support behind it first would be the metaphysical intuition that something cannot come out of nothing out of nothing nothing comes
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig targets Flew’s brute stopping point conditionally: if whatever begins has a cause, the universe cannot be brute, while intuition and uniform experience support that premise. Principal limitation: Observations within a spatiotemporal order do not establish that the principle governs spacetime’s boundary, while calling an uncaused beginning emergence from “nothing” prejudges Flew’s position. Live burden: Craig must justify the domain extension and distinguish nothingness from unexplained initial reality; Flew must identify a principled failure in causal intuition rather than exempting the universe.

moves.sectionTitle: Cosmological causation and the universe’s beginning
moves.currentDescription: Flew distinguishes ordinary small events inside the cosmos from the Big Bang of the cosmos, rejecting Craig’s transfer of familiar causal expectations.
moves.lockedProposition: The causal expectations appropriate to a small event within the universe cannot simply be transferred to the Big Bang of the universe itself.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: make out that um uh there's no difference the little bang and big bang the whole difference is that the little bang occurs within the universe the Big Bang is of the universe itself and Taylor who is uh uh saying
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew isolates the disanalogy: a little bang occurs intracosmically, whereas the Big Bang originates the universe itself, so causal expectations cannot automatically transfer. Principal limitation: Domain difference blocks comparison but does not prove their shared characteristic of beginning causally irrelevant, leaving Craig’s metaphysical principle available unless Flew identifies the decisive difference. Live burden: Flew must specify which spacetime-dependent conditions make causation applicable to small events yet inapplicable to cosmic origination, while Craig must defend trans-spatiotemporal causation independently of the analogy.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Craig emphasizes the delicate balance of life-permitting initial conditions against vastly more numerous prohibiting possibilities, intending their extreme improbability to require explanation.
moves.lockedProposition: Life-permitting universes are vastly less probable than life-prohibiting ones because their initial conditions require an extraordinarily delicate balance.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: depends upon a delicate and complex balance of initial conditions simply given in the Big Bang itself we now know that life prohibiting universes are vastly more probable than any life permitting Universe like ours how much more probable well the answer is that the chances that the Universe should be life permitting are so infinitesimal as to be incomprehensible and incalculable for
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig isolates that life-permitting initial conditions occupy a delicate range against life-prohibiting alternatives, making their occurrence surprising and supporting design. Principal limitation: Calling the odds incalculable without specifying admissible possibilities or a defensible probability measure leaves the inference vulnerable to reference-class, selection-effect, and unknown-law objections and cannot identify agency. Live burden: Craig must define the comparison space and distribution, address observational selection, and establish design over chance or necessity, while Flew must explain why specified life-permission remains unsurprising if those foundations are supplied.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Flew says artifacts are identified through independent knowledge of artifacts, while complex organisms can arise through unconscious forces, weakening Craig’s complexity-to-design comparison.
moves.lockedProposition: Artifacts are recognized as designed because they are artifacts, not merely because they are complex; complex organisms arise through unconscious natural forces.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: by an intelligent being is not the complexity it's simply uh that it is an artifact obviously an artifact and not a natural phenomen the most complicated sophisticated entities in the whole universe are entities of a sort of which I about 3,000 around here and they were not at least within the universe itself designed they were at least within the universe itself we were products of unconscious physical and mechanical forces this argument for Design Within
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew distinguishes recognized artifacts from organisms produced through unconscious physical forces, providing a counterexample to an inference that complexity alone establishes intelligent design. Principal limitation: Craig’s evidence concerns specified life-permitting cosmic conditions and comparative improbability, not organismal complexity, so evolution only partially contacts the inference, while identifying artifacts as artifacts risks circularity without an independent criterion. Live burden: Flew must show why fine-tuning lacks design significance if probabilistically defensible, while Craig must articulate a noncircular detection standard when no universe is known to be manufactured.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Craig divides fine-tuning explanations among law, chance, and design, excludes the first two, and therefore infers design as the best remaining explanation.
moves.lockedProposition: Because cosmic fine-tuning is not due to law or chance, design is its best explanation.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: due to either law chance or design two it is not due to either law or chance three therefore it is due to design number three objective moral
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig presents an auditable eliminative inference: if law, chance, and design exhaust fine-tuning’s explanations, excluding the first two makes design follow, connecting conditions to God’s existence. Principal limitation: The excerpt neither demonstrates the trilemma’s exhaustiveness nor supplies evidence eliminating law and chance, and offers no likelihood or predictive specificity showing that design explains observations better. Live burden: Craig must defend the option set, articulate a principled probability model, and derive distinctive designer expectations, while Flew must identify a credible rival explanation rather than rest solely on skepticism.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Flew argues cosmic probabilities have neither known propensities nor a frequency class of other universes, so Craig has not warranted fine-tuning’s numerical chance premise.
moves.lockedProposition: Probability theories cannot be applied beyond the universe because neither relevant propensities nor a frequency class of other universes is available.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: applying probabilities uh to out again outside the universe makes it impossible I think uh to apply either sort of probability Theory either the propensity Theory because we don't know anything about the propensities of the um objects considered and we certainly can't apply a frequency Theory uh because uh uh we um uh haven't got any other universes
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew directly challenges Craig’s chance-elimination premise: without cosmic propensities or a frequency class of other universes, probability interpretations cannot ground claims of astronomically unlikely fine-tuning. Principal limitation: Showing that propensity and frequency interpretations lack inputs does not establish every epistemic, Bayesian, or model-relative assignment as illegitimate, nor answer qualitative comparison based on relative surprise. Live burden: Flew must demonstrate why no principled measure sustains Craig’s comparison, while Craig must specify his measure, justify its assumptions, and show the design inference remains robust across reasonable alternatives.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Craig denies physical necessity and plausible chance for the initial conditions, intending their razor-edge life-permitting balance to make intelligent design the best explanation.
moves.lockedProposition: The initial conditions are neither physically necessary nor plausibly due to chance, so their razor-edge balance is best explained by design.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: conditions there is nothing in present ideas about laws of initial conditions remotely to suggest that their consistency with the laws of physics would imply uniqueness far from it it seems then that the physical Universe does not have to be the way it is it could have been otherwise and I showed that in fact the universe is balancing on a Razor's Edge that cries out for some sort of explanation it can't be from law it can't be from chance because the chances of this occurring are simply incomprehensible and therefore the best explanation is design now Dr flu says
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig distinguishes necessity from chance, invokes physics against required conditions, and presents life-permitting contingency as favoring design while rejoining Flew’s objection. Principal limitation: Contingency rebuts necessity without establishing design, since “incomprehensible” improbability supplies neither a probability distribution nor assessment of observer selection, undiscovered mechanisms, and designer predictions. Live burden: Craig must provide likelihoods demonstrating design predicts life-permitting conditions better than chance, selection, or unknown law; Flew must identify what evidence could warrant design without universes or designer-production knowledge.

moves.sectionTitle: Fine-tuning and design inference
moves.currentDescription: Craig answers Flew’s artifact criterion by treating specified improbability as a general design signature and applying that comparison to life-permitting cosmic conditions.
moves.lockedProposition: Artifacts are detected through specified improbability, the same signature present in cosmic fine-tuning.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: the question is how do we recognize something as an artifact well we we do so by recognizing a specified improbability about that for example two archaeologists digging in the ground finding certain rocks shaped like uh arroe heads or other implements don't say oh look how the processes of sedimentation and metamorphosis have created these uncanny rocks they immediately recognize the presence of design because of the improbability of
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig answers Flew’s challenge by proposing specified improbability as design evidence and using implements to show unlikelihood supporting inference beyond complexity. Principal limitation: The analogy neither defines specification nor supplies probability distribution or designer likelihood, while arrowhead identification depends upon knowledge of agents and production processes unavailable for universe selection. Live burden: Craig must demonstrate life-permitting conditions meet a noncircular specification and discriminate design from selection or undiscovered law; Flew must engage the criterion rather than reiterating artifact recognition.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Craig distinguishes evolved taboo from genuine wrongness, arguing that atheistic human origins cannot provide objective authority and intending morality to require God.
moves.lockedProposition: Without God, evolved human morality has no objective authority and even acts such as rape are not really wrong.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: question is if God does not exist do objective moral values exist like Russell and Roose I don't see any reason to think that in the absence of God the her morality evolved by Homo sapiens is objective after all if there is no God then what's so special about human beings they're just accidental byproducts of nature which have evolved relatively recently on an infinitesimal Speck of dust lost somewhere in a hostile and Mindless universe and which are doomed to perish individually and collectively in a relatively short time on the atheistic view some action say rape may not be socially advantageous and so in the course of human development has become taboo but that does absolutely nothing to prove that rape is really wrong on the atheistic view there's nothing really wrong with your raping someone thus without God there is no absolute right and wrong
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig distinguishes moral knowledge and conduct from ontological grounding, arguing from humanity’s evolutionary contingency and rape’s adaptive taboo toward atheism’s inability to confer authority. Principal limitation: This genealogy-to-truth inference remains unsupported because biological origins neither disprove secular moral realism nor exclude agency-based reasons and nondivine foundations, which Craig never evaluates. Live burden: Craig must establish divine grounding’s superiority without conflating causal provenance with justification, while Flew must explain how shared standards become categorically binding.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Flew compares finite human offenses with endless punishment, arguing that infinite consequences violate proportional justice and burden claims about a perfectly good God.
moves.lockedProposition: Infinite punishment cannot be justly proportionate to any offense committed during a finite human life.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: crime uh look the punishment needs to be to some extent proportionate to the seriousness of the crime and how could there be any offense committed by a human being in a short life that deserve a literally infinite um punishment so
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew applies proportionality to the mismatch between wrongdoing during a finite lifetime and infinite punishment, challenging compatibility with perfect divine goodness. Principal limitation: The inference presupposes endless retribution for offenses without establishing Craig’s commitment to doctrine or considering rejection, self-exclusion, offense gravity, and nonretributive interpretations. Live burden: Flew must connect infinite punishment to Craig’s God-concept and answer desert theories, while Craig must reconcile endless consequences with finite agency, proportional justice, and goodness.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Craig invokes evident objective wrongs and goods, combines their reality with claimed divine dependence, and infers that God exists as morality’s necessary foundation.
moves.lockedProposition: Objective moral values are real; combined with their dependence on God, this entails that God exists.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: objective values do exist and deep down I think we all know it there's no more reason to deny the objective reality of moral values than the objective reality of the physical world actions like rape cruelty and child abuse aren't just uh socially unacceptable Behavior they are moral Abominations some things are really wrong similarly love equality and self- sacrifice are really good thus we can summ this third consideration as follows premise one if God does not exist objective moral values do not exist two objective values do exist three therefore God
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig completes a conditional syllogism: objective moral values exist, illustrated by rape, cruelty, child abuse, love, equality, and self-sacrifice, and their asserted dependence on God entails divine existence. Principal limitation: These examples distinguish morality from acceptability, but demonstrate neither mind-independent objectivity nor the indispensable premise that atheism cannot accommodate objective value, so the inference inherits that controversy. Live burden: Craig must defend uniquely divine grounding against secular realism and command-independence objections, while Flew must articulate a naturalistic foundation preserving normativity rather than merely citing shared standards.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Flew argues that omnipotence should permit God to create persons who freely choose obedience, challenging the compatibility of divine power, punishment, and wrongdoing.
moves.lockedProposition: An omnipotent God who demands belief under threat of punishment could instead create persons who freely choose obedience.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: mean well now but granted the resources of omnipotence uh I think I could manage uh this um but apparently um the uh God whom the Dr Craig is asking us to believe as the Creator um very much wants people to believe in a certain way and he wants this so much that he's prepared to torture them forever to punishment by not obeying me well it seems to me that anyone who um knew that that was what this Cosmic Saddam Hussein wanted would behave like the sensible subject of hin they'll say anything about his merits and goodness oh yes well wouldn't you if you were going to fall into the hands of his torturers but omnipotent could avoid all this by simply uh making them creatures such that they would choose to obey him how
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew exposes tension among omnipotence, desired obedience, freedom, and punishment by asking why power could not constitute persons who choose obedience without coercion. Principal limitation: The proposal assumes, without a freedom theory, that guaranteed right choice remains libertarianly free; ensuring obedience may eliminate alternatives, while the tyrant comparison caricatures divine rationale. Live burden: Flew must specify a mechanism for certain yet free obedience, while Craig must explain why omnipotence and foreknowledge cannot actualize free right choices and why punishment remains compatible with divine perfection.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Craig says libertarian freedom excludes causal determination and that not every possible world is feasible, blocking Flew’s proposed guarantee of freely chosen obedience.
moves.lockedProposition: Omnipotence cannot make someone freely act, because libertarian freedom excludes causal determination and not every possible world is feasible for God.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: it is logically impossible to make someone freely do something libertarian freedom in entails freedom from causal restraints and therefore if we are truly free and God is Will to create free creatures then he cannot guarantee how free creatures will choose in other
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig identifies the decisive inference: libertarian freedom excludes causal determination, so omnipotence cannot guarantee free choices; distinguishing logically possible from creature-feasible worlds directly answers Flew’s obedient-creation proposal. Principal limitation: This conceptual evidence yields contradiction only assuming libertarianism, without independently vindicating it or explaining why omniscience could not select agents whose foreknown undetermined choices remain consistently good. Live burden: Craig must defend libertarian alternatives and feasibility constraints, while Flew must explain how noncoercive divine influence guarantees right conduct without determination or substitution of compatibilism.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Flew distinguishes coercion from divine constitution, invoking Aquinas to argue that God could move a person’s will toward right action without violating freedom.
moves.lockedProposition: Flew did not propose coercion: an omnipotent God could constitute people so they freely choose rightly, as Aquinas says God can move the will without violence.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: course there is but I didn't say that God should coers people force them to do it I said that God the omnipotent God uh could um uh be able to make people such that they would freely choose now you may say this is the doctrine of predestination and of course only Calvinists believe that not true uh this uh view uh that it made perfectly good sense to say and indeed it was the truth to say uh that uh God guided the wills both of the saved and the damned is found in for instance a coinus I quote I've got a lot of quotations here but still we'll stick with one God Alone can move the will as an agent without doing violence to it
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew corrects Craig’s coercion reconstruction and supplies Thomistic evidence for the alternative that divine agency can constitute or move willing according to its nature without external violence, restoring the freely-obedient-creation challenge. Principal limitation: Aquinas establishes an available model, not that infallibly moved action preserves Craig’s libertarian alternatives; consequently, Flew risks changing freedom theories without defeating Craig’s inference internally. Live burden: Flew must distinguish constitution, guidance, determination, voluntariness, and genuine freedom to show guaranteed goodness is noncoercive, while Craig must justify treating libertarianism and feasibility constraints as controlling.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Craig concedes Flew’s point under Thomistic concurrence but adopts Molinist cooperation, where God acts with rather than moves the will, preserving libertarian alternatives.
moves.lockedProposition: Flew’s reply presupposes Thomistic concurrence, but on Molinist libertarianism God acts with rather than moves the will, preserving genuine alternatives.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: lift my arm and I agree if that's the way you think of God's working then Dr flu is Right omnipotence could bring it about that everyone would freely do what God wants them to do but on Molina's view God's concurrence acts to produce the secondary effect with my will but he does not move on my will to produce the effect because Molina argued that would be incompatible with human Freedom then
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig grants Flew’s conclusion under Aquinas, then identifies its theory-dependent premise by contrasting Thomistic premotion with Molina’s concurrence: God produces the effect alongside, rather than moving, the creaturely will, preserving alternatives. Principal limitation: This is a model-dependent escape, since middle knowledge, libertarian counterfactuals, and concurrence with unpremoved choice remain insufficiently justified, while divine responsibility for world-selection is unresolved. Live burden: Craig must substantiate modal commitments and reconcile world-selection with responsibility; Flew must challenge Molinism instead of assuming Thomistic concurrence uniquely governs omnipotent action.

moves.sectionTitle: Morality, freedom, hell, and divine goodness
moves.currentDescription: Flew grounds objective judgments in standards common to humanity, arguing that acts can be genuinely wrong without becoming wrong solely through divine command.
moves.lockedProposition: Moral judgments appeal to standards common to humanity and can be objectively true without being true only because God commands or approves them.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: as hum put it appealing to some standards common to all mankind and saying no this is not a matter of uh my dislikes and likes or my interests it's a matter of something else um and I I think the uh I I'm perfectly to be prepared happy to believe constantly maintaining things that things are really wrong and so on but I don't think uh they're wrong and only wrong and only really wrong because God said so and I certainly
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew concedes morality yet denies Craig’s grounding conditional, invoking Hume’s common standards to distinguish wrongness from dislike and question whether objectivity requires divine command. Principal limitation: Common standards may explain agreement without establishing mind-independent authority; Flew neither shows why standards bind nor addresses error, while reducing Craig’s grounding thesis to command dependence narrows its claim. Live burden: Flew must provide a nondivine account of normative truth and obligation; Craig must show divine grounding supplies necessity and avoids arbitrariness.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Craig connects Jesus’s claimed divine authority with resurrection, arguing that a genuine rising from death would constitute miraculous evidence for God’s existence.
moves.lockedProposition: Jesus acted with divine authority, and his resurrection would constitute miraculous evidence for God.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: came on the scene with an unprecedented sense of divine Authority the authority to stand and speak in God's place he claimed that in himself the kingdom of God had come and as visible demonstrations of this fact he carried out a Ministry of Miracles and exorcisms but the Supreme confirmation of his claim was his resurrection from the dead if Jesus did rise from the dead then it would seem that we have a Divine Miracle on our hands and thus evidence for the existence of God now most people
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig states the conditional inference precisely: if Jesus, having claimed divine authority, genuinely rose, that extraordinary event would provide direct evidence of divine agency and God. Principal limitation: The bridge establishes neither resurrection nor uniquely divine causation, since legendary development, unknown processes, or alternative agents remain possible without defended testimony and causal comparison. Live burden: Craig must substantiate the event and demonstrate why God’s miracle outperforms alternatives, while Flew must show why the facts fail proportionate historical standards or favor another explanation.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Flew applies stringent anomalous-report standards to resurrection documents written roughly thirty years later, arguing that their distance from events makes supernatural confidence unjustified.
moves.lockedProposition: Resurrection documents appearing about thirty years after the alleged events fall well below the evidential standard Flew applied to anomalous reports.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: evence the uh most recent documentation after the alleged events were 30 or so years afterwards when I was an active member of the society for psychological research uh we would have had grave doubts about uh taking as an absolutely faithful record documents that were say a year or so later than the actual event and what have we got by way of evidence
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew presents a concrete source-critical inference: documentation appearing approximately thirty years after the alleged resurrection warrants reduced confidence, especially against his stricter standard for anomalous reports in psychical research. Principal limitation: Delay alone cannot establish unreliability, and the reply does not examine tradition age, source independence, multiple attestation, or Craig’s empty-tomb, appearance, and transformed-belief claims. Live burden: Flew must connect lateness to specific defects in those premises, while Craig must demonstrate reliable transmission adequate for an extraordinary historical conclusion.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Craig presents the empty tomb and postmortem appearances to individuals and groups as established historical facts requiring comparison among naturalistic and supernatural explanations.
moves.lockedProposition: The empty tomb and postmortem appearances to individuals and groups are established historical facts.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: but there are actually three established facts recognized by the majority of New Testament historians today which I believe are best explained by the resurrection of Jesus fact number one on the Sunday following his crucifixion Jesus tomb was found empty by a group of his women followers according to yakob Kramer an Austrian scholar who has specialized in the study of the Resurrection quote by far most Scholars hold firmly to the reliability of the biblical statements about the empty tomb end quote fact number two on separate occasions different individuals and groups saw appearances
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig isolates empty-tomb and appearance reports as independently inspectable historical data, invoking scholarly agreement and distinguishing premises intended to make resurrection explanatorily preferable. Principal limitation: “Established facts” outruns his warrant because he analyzes neither source independence, burial tradition, narrative development, nor whether early experiences support the embodied encounters his inference requires. Live burden: Craig must validate each datum under ordinary historical criteria and demonstrate resurrection’s comparative superiority, while Flew must answer them separately and substantiate source-critical alternatives.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Flew contrasts early Pauline letters and their visionary appearances with later bodily narratives, arguing that chronological development weakens Craig’s unified resurrection evidence.
moves.lockedProposition: The earliest New Testament documents are Pauline letters, whose sparse detail and visionary appearances differ from later bodily narratives.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: uh uh first um uh first New Testament documents were Pauline Epistles rather than the gospels and what is so remarkable about the Pauline comp Epistles is what they don't say about the detail of Jesus and how the appearances uh recorded were apparently Visions which is a very different thing
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew challenges Craig’s appearance premise chronologically: earlier Pauline letters are sparse and portray experiences he considers visionary, unlike later embodied-encounter narratives. Principal limitation: Calling Paul’s reports visions does not prove a nonbodily conception, because Flew quotes no passages, examines no early creed, and never tests continuity with Gospel traditions. Live burden: Flew must document development from visionary experience to bodily narrative and its inferential significance, while Craig must show earliest sources support the same event and bodily conception as later accounts.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues that contrary Jewish expectations make the disciples’ transformative resurrection conviction historically surprising, intending their changed belief to demand a powerful explanation.
moves.lockedProposition: The disciples adopted resurrection belief despite contrary Jewish expectations, with a transformative conviction that historians must explain.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: having every predisposition to the contrary Jews had no belief in a dying much less a rising Messiah and Jewish beliefs about the afterlife precluded anyone's rising from the dead before the end of the world nevertheless the or origal disciples suddenly came to believe in the resurrection of Jesus so strongly that they were willing to die for the truth of that belief Luke Johnson a new testament scholar from Emory University Muses some sort of powerful transformative experience is required to generate the sort of movement earliest Christianity was and T Wright an eminent British uh scholar concludes that is why as an historian I cannot explain the rise of early Christianity unless Jesus rose again leaving an empty tomb behind him
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig converts the disciples’ unexpected resurrection belief, contrary to Jewish expectations, into an explanandum, reinforced by transformative conviction and judgments from Johnson and Wright. Principal limitation: Unexpected belief and transformation do not uniquely establish bodily resurrection; Jewish expectations, grief experiences, cognitive reinterpretation, group dynamics, and developing tradition remain inadequately documented or comparatively assessed. Live burden: Craig must substantiate these claims and show resurrection outpredicts natural and social pathways, while Flew must present a historically supported alternative rather than abstract possibility.

moves.sectionTitle: Historical evidence for Jesus’s resurrection
moves.currentDescription: Craig argues that calling evidence insufficient leaves the empty tomb, appearances, and transformed belief unexplained, burdening Flew to provide a plausible comparative naturalistic account.
moves.lockedProposition: Calling the evidence insufficient does not explain the empty tomb, appearances, and disciples’ belief; no plausible naturalistic alternative was supplied.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: him of doing he simply says the evidence is insufficient but he doesn't engage himself with the evidence remember I pointed out that critical New Testament historian agree that the empty tomb the postmortem appearances and the origin of the disciples Faith are all established historical facts so I'm asking Dr flu what is a better explanation of those than the fact that these men were telling the truth that Jesus did rise from the dead is he going to defend that uh there was a conspiracy is he going to say Jesus wasn't really dead I mean what is his alternative it seems to me that there is no plausible naturalistic alternative to that finally let me just
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig distinguishes evidential insufficiency from explaining the empty tomb, postmortem appearances, and disciples’ faith, making Flew’s undeveloped naturalistic account pertinent comparatively. Principal limitation: A skeptic need not supply an alternative when Craig has not secured resurrection’s factual basis or comparative superiority, and this framing bypasses Flew’s delayed-document and Pauline-vision arguments. Live burden: Craig must defend the explananda and show resurrection outpredicts natural mechanisms, while Flew should specify facts granted, how source criticism undermines them, and why no unified alternative is required.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Craig treats immediate experience of God as potentially warranting belief without argument, comparing it to inescapable experiential reality rather than an adopted intellectual idea.
moves.lockedProposition: God can be known apart from argument through immediate experience treated as an inescapable experiential reality rather than a mere idea.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: the claim that you can know that God exists wholly apart from arguments simply by immediately experiencing him this was the way that people in the Bible knew God as professor John hick explains God was known to them as a dynamic will interacting with their own Wills a sheer given reality as inescapably to be reckoned with as destructive storm and life-giving sunshine to them God was not an idea adopted by the mind but an experiential reality which gave significance to their
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig separates public demonstration from immediate experiential warrant, using encounters and Hick’s comparison with inescapable realities to explain how awareness could prima facie justify theistic belief. Principal limitation: These illustrations establish psychological immediacy, not veridical identification, because inference from experience to God remains vulnerable to perceptual error, incompatible religious encounters, and nonconfirmation. Live burden: Craig must provide reliability tests and explain how private warrant advances the motion; Flew must address justification without miscasting it as proof.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Flew limits his burden to showing insufficient reasons for belief rather than disproving God, criticizing Craig’s confidence about knowing what caused the universe.
moves.lockedProposition: Flew’s case is not that God is disproved but that Craig lacks sufficient reasons and is too bold about knowing the universe’s cause.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: no sufficient reasons for believing that there is and uh Dr Craig apparently was wanting to maintain the exact opposite uh that I wouldn't be able to establish that there is no God uh but he thinks he's provided sufficient reasons for thinking that there is now he has offered so many arguments that it will be impossible for me in any reasonable amount of time to answer them all but uh what I'm going to say if it's right will provide a sufficient reason for thinking uh that he and others are altogether too bold in thinking uh that uh they know
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew distinguishes insufficient justification from disproof of God, an inference tracking the motion’s evidential burden and representing Craig as claiming sufficient reasons. Principal limitation: This framing is not substantive refutation: calling Craig overly bold requires epistemic standards and targeted reasons why his considerations fail cumulatively, rather than observing that replies are impracticable. Live burden: Flew must convert withholding into objections addressing premises and cumulative force, while Craig must show evidence crosses a threshold without transferring an obligation to prove nonexistence.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Craig contrasts mental and physical properties to resist reductive materialism, intending the possibility of an immaterial self to support a personal incorporeal cosmic cause.
moves.lockedProposition: Mental properties differ from physical properties in kind, so reductive materialism does not rule out an immaterial personal cause.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: because mental properties are clearly distinct from physical properties for example the brain is not sad but a person is sad a mental property is different than a physical property a thought doesn't have a weight or a spatial location so reductive materialism just won't work what about
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig uses sadness belonging to persons rather than brains and thoughts lacking weight or location to distinguish mental from physical properties, challenging reductive materialism and preserving an immaterial personal cause. Principal limitation: These contrasts establish neither substance dualism nor disembodied agency and exclude neither nonreductive physicalism nor emergence, leaving the ontological transition unsupported. Live burden: Craig must derive an existing immaterial self and connect its agency to the universe’s cause, while Flew must explain why personhood requires embodiment despite irreducible mentality.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Flew argues that if physics identifies nothing before the Big Bang, responsible human knowledge may terminate there rather than posit an unknowable transcendent cause.
moves.lockedProposition: If physics reaches the Big Bang and can identify no earlier cause, human knowledge may simply end there.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: nothing but you know we just not in a position to answer the question and the fact that one is unable to suggest a a cause for the Big Bang why should you think uh that anyone but a physicist is going to explain that and if physics stops there isn't that the end of human knowledge well now let's consider uh the
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew infers that inability to identify a cause earlier than Big Bang warrants agnosticism, treating physics as comparison while avoiding the claim that ignorance proves no cause. Principal limitation: He identifies no physical barrier and never establishes that physical explanation’s stopping point bounds metaphysical inference, so “the end of human knowledge” exceeds his evidence. Live burden: Flew must show why causal reasoning loses warrant beyond physics, while Craig must demonstrate its reliability where empirical access, theory-building, and temporal concepts may fail.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Craig says materialism cannot explain identity, intentionality, or freedom and has not shown unembodied mind impossible, renewing his defense of a personal immaterial cause.
moves.lockedProposition: Material-person claims fail to explain identity, intentionality, and free will and do not show an unembodied mind impossible.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: epiphenomenalism on that view you cannot explain self-identity over time you cannot explain intentionality you cannot explain free will uh none of that makes sense so I think that's an inadequate View in any case he's never shown that there cannot be a an unembodied personal mind and uh therefore I don't think he's
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Craig contests Flew’s material-person premise by identifying diachronic identity, intentionality, and free agency as failures for epiphenomenalism, keeping an unembodied personal cause available. Principal limitation: These challenges reveal explanatory pressure, because they neither compare materialist alternatives nor establish an immaterial self, a bodyless mind’s possibility, or the morally interested God Flew disputes. Live burden: Craig must supply the bridge from mental phenomena to a cosmic agent, while Flew must defend material personhood and explain why gaps support no modal opening.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Flew grants arguendo a cause with some unusual attributes but denies that Craig has reached the standard God or established divine concern with human morality.
moves.lockedProposition: Even if a cause had some divine attributes, Craig has not justified the full standard God-concept or its supposed interest in human morality.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: that's a lot of characteristics for this cause that uh some of the audience clearly think got it that's what it must have caused the whole universe well it's a lot of things it would be perfectly possible uh that there should be a a being that uh was was omnipotent omniscient uh but wasn't particularly interested in human conduct um of course of course everyone thinking of creation um uh is thinking of the first uh um uh two chapters of Genesis well the Creator God there created the whole universe in order to have some human beings in created in His image but why should we assume in this definition of God uh that um he has this interest
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew exposes the attribute-bridging gap through a counterexample: even a universe-causing being with power or knowledge need not possess moral concern, so a cosmic cause does not entail the standard God-concept. Principal limitation: The objection bundles properties and leans on Genesis framing, insufficiently engaging Craig’s personal-agency inference, cumulative moral case, and resurrection route; it restricts the cosmological conclusion without defeating the case. Live burden: Flew must test bridges individually, while Craig must justify additional attributes and explain why causal, personal, moral, and providential conclusions converge on a being.

moves.sectionTitle: Religious experience, personhood, and epistemic burden
moves.currentDescription: Flew distinguishes testimony that an experience occurred from evidence that its apparent divine object was real, denying religious experience independent public authority.
moves.lockedProposition: A subject’s testimony establishes that an experience occurred, not that it involved a real God; religious experience therefore lacks external authority.
moves.completeLockedSourceExcerpt: subject's uh uh testimony is not authoritative of course it's authoritative if we're asking uh whether they had the experience in the Philosopher's sense the honest testimony is the last word but when someone says they had an experience of dealing with cows and so on um that means they've actually had dealings with real cows well uh so much for the appeal to
moves.assessmentRationale: Strongest feature: Flew distinguishes authority that an experience occurred from authority that its object exists, using the cow comparison to expose the inference from phenomenology to veridical divine encounter. Principal limitation: This evidence restricts testimony as public proof but neither demonstrates unreliability nor identifies defeaters sufficient to withhold personal warrant extended to perception. Live burden: Flew must articulate reliability criteria and defeaters, while Craig must supply discriminators separating divine contact from hallucination, projection, or incompatible revelation and explain why immediacy bridges the evidential gap.
